newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians see rewards and risks of revamped rouble.
newsitem.headline: Russians see rewards and risks of revamped rouble.

text.p: Russians, seasoned to the shock tactics that have marked their country's hectic transition to a market economy, gave a wary welcome on Monday to government plans to lop off three zeroes from the much inflated rouble.
President Boris Yeltsin announced that Russia would redenominate the rouble from January 1 1998, introducing a new rouble worth 1,000 old ones.
"This is basically a positive step," said Robert Eksuzyan, a Muscovite in his sixties.
"When things are calculated in billions and even trillions, it reminds me of the days my father spoke of in the 1920s, when people had to carry around sackfuls of money."
Some were more wary of the government's plans, mindful of Soviet-era redenominations which could turn savings to worthless paper overnight.

"I've lived here all my life, and I know that if the government promises one thing, they turn it around 180 degrees. They want to steal from the people, and everyone is tired of being tricked," said an elderly man who asked not to be named.
Prices are not quite as inflated in the 1990s as they were in the 1920s.
But they can still be baffling, especially for the older generation which used to pay for basic food in kopecks but now has to fork out tens of thousands of roubles.
A loaf of bread which cost 25 kopecks -- a quarter of one rouble -- in the late 1980s now costs around 2,500 roubles, or 10,000 times as much.

Prices skyrocketed in the early 1990s when the planned economy was scrapped and prices were freed. Inflation reached four figures annually in late-1993 and the rouble has plunged from 0.55 to the U.S. dollar to 5,800 today.

Lopping three zeroes off the rouble is partly aimed at curing people of a deeply-ingrained inflationary mentality, still prevalent in the Russian consciousness, that encourages many to change roubles into dollars at the first possible opportunity.
But its practical advantages were not lost on people.
"I think the less roubles the better," said a young man outside the Kiev railway station in central Moscow. "We won't have to do so much maths."
People were keen to see an orderly transition to a new price system from the old.
"As long as prices change accordingly, then everything will be fine," said an elderly lady.
But not everyone agreed the transition would be fair.
"There is a good chance the government will try to pocket some money in the process by not dropping prices accordingly," said a middle-aged woman running a small electrical shop.
But few Russians seemed to expect a repetition of the panic triggered by previous currency reforms.

Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev prompted outrage in 1961 when he made 10 roubles worth one. Angry Russians queued for hours outside shops to stock up on basic provisions before the new rate was pushed through.
And in 1991 people were forced to swap old high-denomination rouble notes for new ones in just three days. Millions lost life savings overnight as a result of the drastic deflationary step.
Yeltsin said he wanted to avoid the mistakes of the past.
"In the last 50 years, everything connected with monetary reform always hit ordinary people here. Now that is ruled out. As president, I guarantee this," he said on Monday.
To avoid pandemonium, Yeltsin said people were not obliged to change old notes for new. The redenomination would start on January 1, 1998 and old notes would be usable throughout 1998.
After that, Russians would have another four years to exchange old roubles for new, Yeltsin said.
